questions.explain: The rehost/replatform/retain classification drives the wave plan and target selection for every database.
options: Rehost (lift-and-shift to EC2/VMs), replatform (to RDS/Azure SQL/MI), or retain/replace (stays on-premises or the app is being replaced)
Large, medium, or small — based solely on database size
Critical, important, or optional — based solely on business priority
OLTP, analytics, or archival — based on workload type
questions.q: In the migration assessment, how should each database be classified?

questions.explain: Log shipping/differential catch-up gives minutes of downtime for large databases: the seed restores early and log restores catch up before cutover.
options: Distributed AG, because it works with managed-service targets
Native backup/restore with hours of downtime, since it is the universal fallback
Log shipping / differential catch-up — the seed restores early and logs catch up, leaving minutes of downtime
Transactional replication, which requires seconds of downtime
questions.q: For a large database where a small maintenance window exists, which migration method fits and why?

questions.explain: Wave zero migrates non-production, low-risk databases to prove the pipeline, tooling, and runbook before production waves.
options: Decommissioning the source servers before any migration begins
Load-testing the target with synthetic workloads before production moves
Migrating the most critical production databases first to get them stable
Migrating non-production, low-risk databases first to prove the pipeline, the tooling, and the runbook
questions.q: What is the purpose of wave zero in the wave plan?

questions.explain: The cutover script drains to zero lag, restores the final logs, runs DBCC CHECKDB (the restore you trust), redirects clients, and runs smoke tests on the business's critical transactions.
options: Run the final differential/log backup and restore, run DBCC CHECKDB on the target, redirect connection strings, then run the business smoke-test suite
Redirect clients first, then restore the final backup while the application is connected
Rebuild all indexes before cutover and skip integrity checks to save time
Stop the source, take a full backup, and delete the source database immediately
questions.q: Which steps are part of the cutover script's final phase on the target?

questions.explain: The source stays intact and replication-capable for the rollback window (typically 24–72 hours) until the migration is declared successful.
options: Rollback is never planned for backup/restore migrations, only replication-based ones
Decommission the source immediately after cutover to save licensing costs
Keep the source database intact and replication-capable until the migration is declared successful — typically 24–72 hours
Take a final backup of the source and shut it down within one hour of cutover
questions.q: What is the rollback window discipline for the source database?
